The removable saint and the removable felon stand in the same posture before &sect;237, differentiated only by the relief each can reach—and the desk notes, as a matter of the same record, that the relief map is itself drawn in conduct: the felon’s aggravated felony closes doors the saint’s clean record leaves open. The system is not indifferent to virtue out of absent-mindedness. It is built so that virtue is currency in the relief market and legal tender nowhere else.

The public debate poses its version of the question through a hypothetical: a figure of universal charitable reputation—the standing example is Mother Teresa of Calcutta, Albanian-born, a citizen of India, founder of the Missionaries of Charity—entering the United States to do religious work without status. On the statute as written, she would be removable, because the grounds in section 3 would apply to her as to anyone, and her works would appear in her case only as equities in a discretionary request. The record files what the hypothetical leaves out. A dedicated lawful channel exists for exactly her case and has for generations: the R-1 nonimmigrant classification at &sect;101(a)(15)(R) admits religious workers—ministers and persons in religious vocations, members of a denomination with a bona fide nonprofit religious organization in the United States, coming to work for it—for up to five years, and the EB-4 special-immigrant category admits religious workers to permanent residence. And the historical case itself ran through the law’s front door and past it: by Public Law 104-218, enacted October 1, 1996, Congress conferred honorary citizenship of the United States on her, making her one of eight persons so honored in the republic’s history and one of two—with Winston Churchill, in 1963—honored in her lifetime. The State Department’s own manual (8 FAM 306.1) records the honor’s legal content: honorary citizenship confers no special entry, travel, or immigration benefits, and its holder is not eligible for a United States passport. Which is to say, the republic’s highest civic compliment left its recipient’s immigration position exactly where the statute put it, and the honor and the removability coexisted in the same file without contradiction, because they answer different questions. The desk files the exhibit at that temperature: the removability grounds ask nothing about character; the channels exist; the actual case used them.

10. “Naturalization”: A Definitions Section

The word does one job in the statute and another in the argument, and the desk files both. In law, naturalization is the defined process by which a person not born a citizen becomes one, at INA &sect;&sect;310–347 (8 U.S.C. &sect;&sect;1421–1459). Its core requirements stand at &sect;316(a): the applicant must be a lawful permanent resident for five years (three, under &sect;319(a), if married to and living with a citizen); must show continuous residence and physical presence for at least half that period; must show good moral character for the statutory period against the &sect;101(f) disqualifiers; must demonstrate English proficiency and knowledge of United States history and government under &sect;312, subject to age, disability, and long-residence exceptions; must show attachment to the principles of the Constitution; and must take the oath of allegiance at &sect;337, renouncing prior allegiances. Citizenship so acquired is near-absolute against the state: it can be undone only by denaturalization in federal court under &sect;340, for illegal procurement or material concealment in the process itself—a door the government has used sparingly and the courts supervise closely. Beside the statutory word stands the colloquial one, in which long residence is said to “naturalize” a person into a place—to make him, in substance, of it—with entitlement argued to follow from the substance. United States law contains no such ripening for the non-resident, and it contains exactly one fossil of the idea: the registry provision, &sect;249, which permits a person of good moral character present since a fixed date to register into residence—a date Congress set at June 28, 1940 in 1929, advanced by stages to June 30, 1948, and last advanced by the Immigration Reform and Control Act of 1986 to January 1, 1972, where it has remained for forty years, a door built for a generation that has now passed through it or died. Residence ripens into status by rule in other systems on the shelf—the European Union’s long-term resident status attaches after five years of legal residence under Council Directive 2003/109/EC—and the desk files the contrast as it files the others: a design choice, present there, absent here, its presence or absence a fact about statutes and not about the worth of the residents.

Acquisition at birth, the other door, runs on two principles whose distribution is itself a ledger. Jus soli—citizenship by birth on the territory—is the rule of the United States under the Fourteenth Amendment and INA &sect;301(a) (“born in the United States, and subject to the jurisdiction thereof”), and of most of the Americas, Canada and nearly all of Latin America included. Jus sanguinis—citizenship by descent—is the rule of most of Europe and Asia, transmitted through a citizen parent wherever the birth occurs; the United States applies it abroad at &sect;301(c)–(g) beside its soil rule. Pure forms are now rare: Germany, the historic sanguinis case, added a soil element in 2000 for children of long-resident foreigners; Ireland restricted its soil rule by referendum in 2004, the last European state to retire an unconditional one; France mixes both with residence-based acquisition at majority; Israel’s Law of Return is a descent-and-identity rule of its own kind. The desk’s observation is bookkeeping: every state on earth assigns membership at birth by some combination of soil and blood and then administers a defined door—naturalization—for everyone else, and the definitions, not the affections of the public, are what the doors are made of. What the colloquial usage asks for is that the door be deemed walked through by time served. No statute on the shelf deems it; some legislatures have built versions of it; the American registry stands in the book with its date unadvanced since 1986.

11. The Public Vocabulary: Two Phrases and a Frame, Examined

The desk applies its definitions instrument to the phrases the argument is conducted in, beginning with the enforcement side’s. “Bad hombres” entered the record in the third presidential debate of October 19, 2016, at Las Vegas, in the Republican nominee’s answer on immigration: “One of my first acts will be to get all of the drug lords, all of the bad ones—we have some bad, bad people in this country that have to go out. We’re going to get them out; we’re going to secure the border. And once the border is secured, at a later date, we’ll make a determination as to the rest. But we have some bad hombres here, and we’re going to get them out.” Grammatically the phrase names a class—in context, the drug lords and the “bad ones”—and the sentence around it makes a testable promise with two parts: enforcement’s first acts would fall on the criminal class, and the disposition of “the rest” would be determined later. The desk tests the promise against the record it has already filed, in section 4’s series, and states the fit plainly: in every year in the series, including the years of explicit priority enforcement before the phrase was coined and the years after, the convicted were a majority of interior removals—82 percent in fiscal 2013, 91 percent in 2015, 93 percent criminal-involved in 2024—and a minority of removals overall wherever the border fast tracks supplied the volume, falling to 32.7 percent conviction-or-charge in fiscal 2024 and lower in 2025, because the majority of the removed in the modern system are processed where they are caught, at the border, a population selected by geography rather than by record. The phrase’s class exists in the data; it has never described the whole of the removed, and in the most recent years it describes the smallest share of them since ICE began publishing the split. Whether that arithmetic honors or betrays the promise of October 2016 is an argument the desk leaves to its makers; the instrument’s reading is that the promise was kept in the interior, where it could be targeted, and swamped in the total, where it could not.

The opposition’s phrase is of a different grammatical species, and the desk files it as what it is: a claim about legitimacy, not about law. “No one is illegal on stolen land”—of uncertain coinage, in mass circulation on signs and murals by the late 2010s—asserts that the enforcing sovereign holds its territory by conquest, and that a title so acquired cannot make presence wrongful. As logic, the premise addresses the legitimacy of the United States’ jurisdiction, not the content of the Immigration and Nationality Act; nothing in the sentence engages &sect;212 or &sect;237, and it would stand or fall identically if both were repealed tomorrow and replaced. As law, it is not cognizable in the forum where removals are decided: an immigration judge’s jurisdiction runs to the statute and the regulations, challenges to the court’s authority over the respondent are resolved against the challenger as a matter of course, and the doctrinal ground was settled a century before the phrase—the federal power over admission and removal is an incident of sovereignty, in the line of cases from the Chinese Exclusion Case, 130 U.S. 581 (1889), through Fong Yue Ting v. United States, 149 U.S. 698 (1893), which held removal to be not punishment but the withdrawal of a privilege of residence, a holding never overruled. The forums in which the premise could be acted on are the legislative and constitutional ones—a Congress persuaded by it could repeal the bars, a constitutional amendment could restructure the power—which is to say the phrase is a political argument wearing a legal sentence’s clothes, and graded as politics it competes with other politics. The desk adds its one filed observation, as comparative record rather than rebuttal: the premise, taken at full strength, runs against every state on earth, since every administering state on the shelf—Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Mexico, and the European states included—governs entry on land acquired by conquest at some depth in its history, and each of them keeps a removals ledger of the kind filed in section 6. A principle that invalidates all of them equally distinguishes none of them, and the desk files it, at that grade, in the ledger.

The third specimen is not a phrase but a frame the two phrases share, stated here in its holders’ strongest form before it is graded. The deservingness frame holds that removal operates, or should operate, as a judgment on the person—that the good should be unremovable because good, and, in its mirror form, that the removed are by the fact of removal shown bad. Its articulated grounds, as its holders state them, are four: family unity—that removal of a parent or spouse inflicts a punishment on citizen family members who have violated nothing, a ground Congress itself has written into the hardship provisions of the statute; the 1986 precedent—that the legislature has once before converted long residence into status at scale, and a mechanism enacted once is a policy available again, not a category error; the prosecutorial-discretion tradition—that enforcement has always ranked its targets, from the deferred-action programs to the priority memoranda of successive administrations, so that selection by equities is the system’s own practice rather than an import; and reliance—that decades of tolerated presence, tax filings accepted under individual taxpayer identification numbers, and licenses issued by the states constitute a course of dealing on which lives were built in reasonable reliance. Graded against the record in this report, the frame in both its directions misdescribes the removability machinery it addresses: the grounds ask nothing about desert (section 9); the criminal series shows the removed to be, in the majority of recent years, persons with no conviction at all (section 4); and the resident’s exposure turns on charging decisions and sentence lines rather than on any assessment of his deserts (section 8). The grounds its holders cite are real—each is documented in the statute, the precedent, or the enforcement record cited—and each operates, where it operates, at the relief, discretion, and legislative stages of the system rather than at the removability stage the frame describes. The desk files the frame at that grade, and proceeds to the scale of the machine itself.

12. Scale: The System in Numbers

The machine’s dimensions, filed with their years and their counters, because the counters disagree in instructive ways. Removals. Counting ICE’s removals only: 142,580 in fiscal 2023; 271,484 in fiscal 2024; about 320,000 in fiscal 2025 by USAFacts’ compilation, 329,018 by the independent reconstruction from ICE’s biweekly releases; and 356,389 in fiscal 2026 through July 11, 2026, by ICE’s figures as reported—against a department-wide DHS removal count of 183,360 for fiscal 2023 and 329,990 for fiscal 2024 in the Office of Homeland Security Statistics’ series, which folds in CBP-executed removals, and a modern single-year record of 438,421 total removals set in fiscal 2013. The two families of numbers measure different machines—one agency’s execution docket against the department’s whole ledger—and any public figure for “deportations” that does not name its counter is filed by this desk as incomplete on its face. The courts. TRAC’s case-level count puts the immigration-court backlog at 3,037,800 pending cases at the end of September 2026, of whom 2,259,317 have filed asylum applications; EOIR’s aggregate tables print higher figures—3,722,776 at the end of fiscal 2025, 3,469,569 at fiscal 2026’s third quarter—the two series counting cases and files by different rules; the Justice Department recorded a decline of more than 447,000 from January 2025 to September 2025 against its own earlier peak above 4.18 million, while immigration judges issued 485,456 removal orders in fiscal 2025, up 57 percent on the year, 306,557 of them in absentia, by the Congressional Research Service’s figures. The court that carries this sits 557 judges, down from 735 at the fiscal 2024 peak. The dockets. ICE’s non-detained docket: above 7.6 million at the end of fiscal 2024; 7.3 million in February 2026 (CRS), carrying an estimated 1.6 million final orders, up from 1,445,549 counted in November 2024. Detention. On July 11, 2026, by TRAC’s tabulation of ICE data, 65,765 people were in ICE detention, of whom 70.6 percent—46,436—had no criminal conviction and 39.8 percent had neither a conviction nor a pending charge; the alternatives-to-detention population stood at 183,181; the detained count had touched roughly 73,000 at its late-2025 peak, a record, against funded capacity built for a fraction of it. The staff. ERO’s deportation officers numbered about 6,100 before 2025; the July 2025 reconciliation act carried $75 billion for ICE, including funding to hire 10,000; federal personnel data put the agency’s total workforce at about 20,000 in December 2025 and 29,000 in July 2026, with nearly 12,000 hired between January 2025 and June 2026, the agency announcing in January 2026 that its officer and agent ranks had grown from 10,000 to 22,000—and more than 2,900 employees departing in the first half of 2026, the highest half-year attrition in the agency’s records. The desk files the growth and the churn in the same line, as the personnel data files them.

13. The Public’s Model: What the Polls Say the Country Thinks the Law Is

The desk grades one more claim set: the public’s own account of what the law should be doing, measured by the pollsters of record. The Pew Research Center’s survey of June 2–8, 2025 found 65 percent of American adults saying there should be a way for immigrants living in the country illegally to stay legally if certain requirements are met—36 percent for a path that includes eligibility for citizenship, 29 percent for permanent residence without citizenship—against 31 percent favoring a national deportation effort. The same question read 64 percent in Pew’s August 2024 survey, down from 75 percent in 2020: the legalization majority is durable and narrowing. Pew’s companion survey of February 24–March 2, 2025 asked the removal question in the form this report has used throughout—all, some, or none—and recorded 32 percent for deporting all, 51 percent for deporting some, 16 percent for deporting none. Inside the selective majority, the sorting is nearly unanimous at the top and collapses as the criteria soften: 97 percent would deport those who committed violent crimes—97 percent of Republicans and 97 percent of Democrats within that group—52 percent those who committed nonviolent crimes, 44 percent those who arrived within the past four years, and 15 percent those who have a job. The Harvard CAPS–Harris polling of July 2025 found 79 percent favoring deportation of those here illegally who have committed crimes. Gallup’s review of February 14, 2025, “The Complex Landscape of Public Opinion on Deportation,” adds the methodological finding the desk files as the section’s caution: six probability polls in January 2025 asking the general deportation question in different wordings produced results from evenly split to 66–32 in favor, and in Gallup’s own earlier reading 70 percent favored a citizenship path with requirements while 47 percent simultaneously favored deporting the same population—the two majorities overlap, because the public is answering about different people under one label.

Stated as a doctrine, the public’s model prices time, work, and family as equity—and the statute prices two of the three in the opposite direction. The polls’ internal structure is consistent across houses and wordings: recency aggravates (the arrival of the last four years is the most deportable non-criminal class polled), employment mitigates nearly to zero, citizen children and long residence suppress support for removal wherever a question names them, and violent crime forfeits everything. It operates, in the language of this report, as a ripening doctrine: presence compounded by conduct becomes a claim. The statute book contains no such doctrine for the unauthorized. Time spent in unlawful presence compounds liability—the &sect;212(a)(9)(B) bars lengthen with it, from three years to ten to, on a reentry, permanent—and residence alone has never adjusted anyone’s status since the registry froze. Exactly one provision in the current book weighs time for the respondent, and the desk prints it precisely because it is the public model’s only statutory relative: cancellation of removal under &sect;240A(b), which requires ten years of continuous physical presence—the statute’s own decade—plus good moral character, plus a showing that removal would cause exceptional and extremely unusual hardship to a citizen or resident spouse, parent, or child, a standard the Board construed in Matter of Monreal-Aguinaga, 23 I&N Dec. 56 (BIA 2001), as hardship substantially beyond what would ordinarily be expected from a relative’s deportation, assessed on the factor line descending from Matter of Anderson, 16 I&N Dec. 596 (BIA 1978)—the qualifying relative’s age, health, and conditions in the destination country among them—all under an annual cap of 4,000 grants. Its ancestor operated at scale once: the Immigration Reform and Control Act of 1986 legalized roughly 2.7 million people on the basis of residence since 1982, and the registry at &sect;249, the older mechanism of the same kind, still stands in the book at its frozen date of January 1, 1972. The desk’s conclusion is that the public is not inventing its doctrine from nothing; it is remembering, in poll answers, a mechanism its legislature last ran in 1986 and last advanced forty years ago—while the operative statute runs, on every day since, in the compounding direction.

14. The Exploitation Ledger: Who Captures the Value of Precarity

A population that cannot safely complain is a priced asset, and the file of who collects on it is adjudicated, not anecdotal. The desk files the case record of this section in the order the machinery runs: the crossing itself, the plants the crossed labor feeds, the visa channels that deliver workers already indebted, and then the two anchor judgments. The anchor judgments come last in that order; the section’s largest adjudicated exhibit is the first of them filed here. After Hurricanes Katrina and Rita, Signal International recruited nearly 500 welders and pipefitters from India into the H-2B guestworker program on promises of permanent residence the program cannot confer. The men paid recruiters and a lawyer between $10,000 and $25,000 each—borrowed, in the record, against land, jewelry, and high-interest village loans—and were charged $1,050 a month to live in guarded labor camps in Mississippi and Texas. On February 18, 2015, a federal jury in David v. Signal International found labor trafficking, forced labor, and racketeering, and awarded more than $14 million to the first five plaintiffs; the case stands among the largest labor-trafficking matters in the country’s record. The Thai file runs parallel: in EEOC v. Global Horizons, the courts found a labor contractor had trafficked hundreds of Thai H-2A farmworkers to Hawaii and Washington farms between 2003 and 2007—passports confiscated, movement restricted, deportation used as the standing threat—entering a pattern-or-practice liability ruling in 2014, $8.7 million in damages in the Hawaii case after settlement offsets (the farms themselves settled for $1.2 million and $2.4 million), and a further $7,658,500 award in the Washington case in 2016. The mechanism both juries priced is written into the criminal code: the forced-labor statute, 18 U.S.C. &sect;1589, names as coercion the threat of serious harm and “abuse or threatened abuse of law or legal process”—which is to say, the threat of deportation itself is an enumerated instrument of the crime. The scale instruments bound the adjudicated floor: the National Human Trafficking Hotline recorded 30,162 substantive signals in 2023, identifying 9,619 potential cases involving 16,999 potential victims, of which 1,558 situations were classified labor trafficking and 1,021 more combined labor and sex trafficking; the Department of Homeland Security counted about 1,300 trafficking investigations and more than 2,300 arrests the same year. Between the hotline’s thousands and the courtroom’s dozens lies the unlitigated balance, whose size no instrument measures—the desk files the floor and the darkness above it in the same sentence, as it found them.

The crossing is the first collection point, and its prices are a matter of sentencing records. In the Central District of California, Eduardo Domingo Renoj-Matul was sentenced in 2025 to 262 months in federal prison after pleading guilty to conspiracy and hostage taking: his organization moved about 20,000 Guatemalans between 2019 and July 2024 at fees of $15,000 to $18,000 a person, collected in Guatemala, and the unpaid were held at a stash house on James M. Wood Boulevard in Los Angeles until the fee was paid—release contingent on payment, which is the definition of the hostage mechanism in commercial form. In the Western District of Texas, Enil Edil Mejia-Zuniga was sentenced in July 2025 to ten years for an organization that moved 2,500 to 3,000 people at $6,500 to $12,000 a head—$16 million to $30 million in receipts by his own admission—through stash houses in Monterrey and Piedras Negras, paying armed guides, drivers, and stash-house operators from the take. The hotel at the end of the crossing is of the same kind: the guilty pleas in the June 2022 San Antonio tractor-trailer case, in which fifty-three people died in a trailer whose air conditioning failed, record fees of up to $15,000 a person. The fee is charged before the labor begins, and it is the balance against which the next collectors in this section—the recruiters, the contractors, the employers—hold their leverage, because a worker who arrives owing five figures cannot walk away from the first workplace that takes him.

The plants the labor feeds are documented by the Labor Department’s own enforcement files, and the recurring defendant is a contractor, not the brand on the building. Packers Sanitation Services Inc., of Kieler, Wisconsin—one of the nation’s largest food-sanitation firms—paid $1,544,076 in civil penalties in February 2023, assessed at $15,138 per child, after the Wage and Hour Division found at least 102 children aged thirteen to seventeen working overnight shifts cleaning back saws, brisket saws, and head splitters with hazardous chemicals at thirteen meat-processing plants in eight states, plants operated by JBS, Tyson, Cargill, and others; at least three of the children were injured. The department’s release does not state what share of the 102 were migrant children, and the desk files the count as the department states it, without the status mix the public account assumes. Fayette Janitorial Service LLC, of Somerville, Tennessee, entered a consent judgment in May 2024 to pay $649,304 after investigators found at least twenty-four children, some thirteen, on overnight sanitation shifts at Seaboard Triumph Foods in Sioux City, Iowa, and at Perdue Farms’ plant in Accomac, Virginia—kill-floor equipment cleaned with corrosive chemicals—and in November 2025 a federal grand jury in the Eastern District of Virginia unsealed an indictment charging former Fayette personnel with conspiring, from October 2020 to January 2024, to supply undocumented workers, children among them, with fraudulent identification to work at the Accomac plant; the criminal case is an indictment, not a verdict, and a fourteen-year-old’s severe arm injury at that plant in February 2022 is what opened the file. Mar-Jac Poultry supplies the fatality. On July 14, 2023, Duvan Tomas Perez, sixteen, a Guatemalan immigrant placed at the company’s Hattiesburg, Mississippi, plant by a staffing agency, was pulled into a still-energized deboning machine while deep-cleaning it, with no lockout device in place; OSHA had proposed $212,646 for the failure, and the company settled in August 2024 for $164,814 with enhanced sanitation-shift supervision and training. The department’s wage division then found, at Mar-Jac’s Jasper, Alabama, plant, minors as young as thirteen, fourteen- and fifteen-year-olds eviscerating poultry, operating forklifts, and working the kill floor on overnight shifts; the consent judgment of May 21, 2025, assessed $385,000, on top of $150,000 assessed after the Mississippi investigation found seven minors in prohibited occupations there. In Ohio, the mechanism ran without a plant defendant: in 2014 and 2015, a labor contractor recruited Guatemalan boys of fourteen and fifteen on promises of good jobs and schooling, smuggled them north, and held them in dilapidated trailers in Marion, Ohio, working twelve-hour days at Trillium Farms’ egg operations—cleaning coops, de-beaking and vaccinating chickens—their paychecks withheld against smuggling debts until the FBI freed eight minors and two adults named in the indictment. The ring’s leader, Aroldo Castillo-Serrano, was sentenced to 188 months; his co-defendants drew ten years, fifty-one months, fourteen months, and shorter terms; Trillium itself was not charged, its labor having arrived, as in the sanitation cases, through a contractor.

The older file of the same industry is a court of appeals opinion, and it records the hiring logic in the employer’s own words. Case Farms’ Morganton, North Carolina, plant was staffed from 1989, when its human-resources manager drove a van to Indiantown, Florida, and recruited Guatemalan refugees from a Catholic parish there—the account is in Leon Fink’s The Maya of Morganton, drawn from the manager’s own interviews, and the reason he gave for preferring Guatemalans was the leverage itself: “Guatemalans can’t go back home. They’re here as political refugees. If they go back home, they get shot.” By the representation election of July 12, 1995, roughly 80 percent of the plant’s 514 eligible voters were Latino, nine in ten of those Guatemalan, and more than 70 percent were noncitizens, on the Fourth Circuit’s own recitation of the record in Case Farms of North Carolina v. NLRB, 128 F.3d 841. The workers struck in May 1995, the union won 238 to 183, the company refused to bargain, and the Board’s bargaining order was enforced by the court in 1997—the legal victory arrived, and no contract followed in the six years of talks that preceded the union’s withdrawal. The safety record is the Labor Department’s: sixty-six inspections between 1988 and 2015 produced citations in forty-two; in August 2015 OSHA assessed $861,500 at the Winesburg, Ohio, plant—two willful, twenty repeat, thirty serious violations—and placed the company in the Severe Violator Enforcement Program; in September 2015 it proposed $424,600 more at Canton, Ohio, where a seventeen-year-old employed by the cleaning subcontractor Cal-Clean lost his lower leg to a chiller machine he was cleaning and a Case Farms employee lost two fingertips the same spring; in December 2015 it proposed a further $462,000 for ammonia-refrigeration failures at the two Ohio plants—more than $1.4 million proposed for the year, in the department’s own arithmetic, each figure a proposal the company contested rather than a sum adjudicated. The pattern across three decades of this file is not a status count; it is a sequence: recruitment aimed at workers whose exit is blocked, a union answered with litigated delay, and the most dangerous cleaning assigned, in the later record, to a subcontractor’s employee.

The personal-service trades file their own version, in which the wage structure itself was the exhibit and the state, not a court, was the respondent. In May 2015, The New York Times’ investigation of New York’s nail salons—more than 150 workers and owners interviewed in four languages—documented the trade’s entry price: new manicurists paying a training fee of about $100 for the job itself, working weeks for tips alone, then starting at $30 or $40 a day, with day rates as low as $10 in the advertisements the paper examined; a majority of the workers interviewed were paid below the minimum wage, overtime was effectively unrecorded, and deductions for mistakes came out of pay—the average New York City manicure then cost about $10.50, roughly half the national figure, and the arithmetic of the price was the arithmetic of the wage. The investigation is journalism, filed in this report’s clippings under its subjective stamp, and it was contested in its particulars by other journalists within the year; what is not contested is the enforcement record it triggered, which is the state’s own. New York’s Labor Department had already found 116 violations in a 2014 sweep of twenty-nine salons. Within days of publication in May 2015 the governor imposed emergency regulations and a multi-agency Nail Salon Industry Enforcement Task Force; legislation signed that July imposed ventilation and protective-equipment rules and required every salon to carry a wage bond or insurance sufficient to cover back-wage awards, so that a judgment for stolen wages would have something to collect against; and on the task force’s first anniversary the state announced investigations opened into more than 450 salons and orders against 143 of them to pay $2 million in unpaid wages and damages to 652 workers. The desk files the sequence as it files the others: a documented wage structure, a state response measured in opened investigations and dollars ordered, and a retail price to the customer that the record ties to the wage structure beneath it.

The exchange-visitor channel runs the same economics at the level of the program’s design, and its two adjudicated exhibits are a warehouse and a courtroom. The J-1 visa is the State Department’s, administered not by the department but by designated private sponsors, who charge the participant program fees—commonly several thousand dollars, paid to the sponsor and its overseas recruiting partners before departure, frequently borrowed—and whose fees the program, uniquely among the guestworker channels, does not prohibit. The Southern Poverty Law Center’s 2014 report Culture Shock, filed as a clipping below, records the resulting inventory from hundreds of interviews: students placed in low-wage, long-hour jobs with little of the cultural content the visa exists for, employers relieved of the payroll taxes the channel exempts, and workers carrying sponsor debt into workplaces they cannot leave without ending their lawful presence. The warehouse exhibit is Hershey’s, and its structure is the section’s mechanism in one address: the Eastern Distribution Center III in Palmyra, Pennsylvania, was Hershey’s building, operated by the logistics contractor Exel, staffed through the SHS Group, which recruited J-1 Summer Work Travel students through the sponsor CETUSA. About four hundred students were put to night-shift work lifting fifty-pound boxes on a fast line at $8.35 an hour, charged about $395 a month for required housing, deducted from pay; on August 17, 2011, they walked out. The Labor Department’s settlement of November 14, 2012, recovered $213,042 in back wages for 1,028 students—the housing deductions had taken pay below the minimum wage and overtime had gone unpaid—and resolved $143,000 in OSHA fines against Exel for noise and safety violations at the facility. Hershey was not cited: it held no payroll in the chain. The State Department’s answer was programmatic—the May 2012 rule, still posted in the program’s exclusions, bars Summer Work Travel placements in warehousing, in goods-producing industries, and in jobs whose hours fall predominantly between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m. The courtroom exhibit is Beltran v. InterExchange, in which the designated sponsors of the J-1 au pair program were sued for conspiring to hold some 100,000 au pairs’ pay at a represented “fixed” rate of $195.75 a week; the sponsors settled in 2019 for $65.5 million, approved by the federal court in Colorado that August, without an adjudication of the conspiracy. The channel’s ordinary employments are documented by the sponsors’ own market: pool-management companies such as High Sierra Pools, operating more than a thousand commercial pools in the mid-Atlantic, recruit J-1 lifeguards by the hundreds each summer through overseas agencies, with employer-arranged housing deducted at published weekly rates, and summer camps and amusement parks staff their seasons from the same pool of students. For those employments the desk finds usage, fee schedules, and the SPLC’s interview record—and no adjudicated case of the kind this section files. Which brings the file to the name the public account attaches to the category.

On the record this section is built from, the amusement-park case does not exist. Disney’s documented immigration-labor litigation runs the other direction: in 2015 Walt Disney World replaced about 250 of its own information-technology employees with workers supplied by the outsourcing firms HCL and Cognizant on H-1B visas, required the departing Americans to train their replacements as a condition of severance, and was investigated by the Labor Department, which closed the matter without a violation—the H-1B workers were the contractors’ employees, not Disney’s, which was the legal point and the whole of it. Of J-1 or H-2B exploitation of foreign workers at Disney’s parks, adjudicated or charged, the desk finds no case in the record; what circulates on the subject is program-usage reporting and advocacy summary, which the desk does not file as findings. The finding the record does support is structural, and it is the one this section has been assembling: at the brand-name end of American leisure and food, the precarious worker is almost never on the brand’s payroll—he is on a sanitation contractor’s at the Tyson plant, a staffing agency’s at Mar-Jac, a logistics contractor’s at Hershey, an outsourcing firm’s at Disney—and the contractor layer is where the department’s penalties, the juries’ verdicts, and the indictments in this file consistently land.

The same tether operates inside the lawful channels, at professional wages, by design of the statute rather than by crime. The H-1B worker’s status is his employer’s petition: lose the job and a regulation of 2017 allows up to sixty days to find a new sponsor, change status, or depart. Behind him stands the employment-based green-card queue, capped at 140,000 a year worldwide with no country permitted more than 7 percent; the Cato Institute’s analysis of the government’s data puts the backlog at roughly 1.8 million people, about 1.1 million of them born in India, and the National Foundation for American Policy’s count of the queue in December 2025—1,264,495 people, 79 percent of them Indian—projects, at current rates, a wait of 179 years for an Indian national entering the second-preference queue today; the October 2026 Visa Bulletin was processing Indian second-preference applications filed in 2013. The result is a class of lawful residents a decade and more deep in American life—mortgages held, citizen children in school, careers compounded—whose presence renews annually at an employer’s pleasure and whose exposure, if the tether breaks, runs through the same overstay arithmetic as section 3’s. No one in this paragraph has violated anything; the precarity is a feature of the channel’s design. The desk closes the section with the pattern the adjudicated record supports: at every level of the system examined in this report at which a capture was litigated, the gap between a person’s economic value and his legal security was captured by someone—by the smuggler in the fee, by the recruiter in the debt, by the employer in the discount and the discipline, by the camp landlord at $1,050 a month a man. The desk files the pattern as the section’s finding, bounded by the cases that compose it; what enforcement or legalization would do to the pattern is a policy question the record does not answer, and the desk does not answer it here.

15. The Error File: Citizens, Wrongful Removals, and the Critics’ Claims on the Same Instrument

The critics’ central factual claim—that the machine removes people it has no authority to remove, including citizens—is documented by the government’s own auditors, at a scale those auditors themselves bound. The Government Accountability Office’s report GAO-21-487 (July 2021), examining fiscal 2015 through the second quarter of fiscal 2020, found that ICE had arrested 674, detained 121, and removed 70 individuals across the period whom its records identified as potential United States citizens; that detainers had been issued against at least 895 potential citizens, about 74 percent of them cancelled before action; and that ICE’s data on citizenship claims were too inconsistently recorded for the counts to be treated as more than floors. TRAC’s separate examination of the longer record counted at least 2,840 people wrongly flagged as removable between 2002 and 2017. Citizenship in these cases typically turns on derived and acquired citizenship through parents—the most documentarily tangled corner of the statute book—and the desk files the auditors’ own caveat with their counts: the record system that produces the removals does not reliably record the claims that would impeach them, so the true figure is unknowable from the published instruments, bounded below by the audits and asserted above them by advocates without an instrument of their own. The claim of wrongful removal of citizens is therefore filed as documented-but-small, with its denominator problem stated, and the claim of its nonexistence is filed, against the GAO, as disproven.

The single most litigated error of the current period is a matter of court record, and the desk files the record. In October 2019 an immigration judge granted Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran national who had entered without inspection in 2011, withholding of removal to El Salvador on a finding of likely persecution there, while leaving a removal order in place as to other countries. On March 15, 2025, he was removed to El Salvador and confined in its CECOT prison. In litigation filed by his family (Abrego Garcia v. Noem, No. 8:25-cv-00951, D. Md.), the acting ICE field office director declared under oath on March 31, 2025, that “[t]hrough administrative error, Abrego-Garcia was removed from the United States to El Salvador,” the removal having been carried out “in good faith based on the existence of a final order of removal” and the withholding grant overlooked. The district court ordered the government to facilitate and effectuate his return; the Supreme Court, on April 10, 2025, required the government to facilitate his release from custody in El Salvador. He was returned to the United States on June 6, 2025—into federal criminal custody, under a Tennessee indictment charging human smuggling, to which he has pleaded not guilty and against which a motion to dismiss for vindictive and selective prosecution is pending; the civil and criminal litigation continue at filing. The desk files the case for the machinery it exhibits and for nothing else: a subsisting court order was not executed by the system that held it, the error was conceded in the government’s own declaration, the judiciary’s corrective process ran for twelve weeks across two court systems and an international negotiation, and its resolution arrived fused with a prosecution. Claims that the case proves the system lawless, and claims that it proves the system self-correcting, are both filed as interpretations; the instrument records the sequence.

The conditions under which the machine holds people are litigated on the same record, and the desk files the litigation beside the error file. Deaths in ICE custody reached 38 in fiscal 2026 on the agency’s published detainee-death reports, the highest annual count in its series, up from 11 in fiscal 2024 and fewer than ten in earlier recent years on the Kaiser Family Foundation’s analysis of the agency’s own death reporting; the same analysis records that most of the 2025–2026 deaths involved people with existing medical conditions whose health deteriorated in custody. The administration’s detention expansion—a detained population that touched roughly 73,000 at its late-2025 peak against funded capacity built for a fraction of it (section 12)—has been accompanied, in 2025, by the winding down of the department’s internal detention-oversight offices, the Immigration Detention Ombudsman among them, a reduction Senate oversight letters of 2026 protest and the department defends as reorganization. The courts have entered the file directly: in late 2025 a federal judge issued a preliminary injunction ordering ICE to provide adequate health care and access to counsel to people detained at the California City facility, the state’s largest, after findings of unsanitary conditions and inadequate medical and mental-health care. The agency’s stated position, in its detention standards and its responses to the oversight letters, is that detainees receive comprehensive medical care, screening within hours of arrival, and round-the-clock emergency care. The desk files the injunction, the death series, and the oversight reduction as the adjudicated and official record of the conditions claim, and the agency’s standards as its stated answer; which account the full record supports, facility by facility, is a question the published instruments answer only in pieces, and the desk files it at that grade.

16. The Ledger

The whole subject, sorted by the state of its evidence. The desk closes the file with the four-column accounting the report has applied throughout, to every side’s claims at the same grade. Verified: established by statute, official record, or adjudication. Documented-but-small: real, proven, and measured against a baseline that bounds its size. Claimed-but-unproven: asserted by named makers, with no instrument at the scale claimed. Disproven: tested by the instrument built to test it and failed.

VerifiedDocumented-but-smallClaimed-but-unprovenDisproven

Unlawful presence is a civil violation, not a crime (Arizona v. United States); improper entry and reentry after removal are crimes (8 U.S.C. &sect;&sect;1325–1326). The ladder runs NTA, hearings, BIA, final order, with expedited, administrative, and reinstatement tracks beside it. A removal order carries 5/10/20-year and permanent bars (&sect;212(a)(9)(A)); voluntary departure carries no removal-order bar. Overstays have exceeded border entries among new unauthorized residents since about 2007 (CMS); 538,548 overstay events were counted in fiscal 2024 (DHS). The Schengen clock is cumulative, 90 in 180, and Switzerland is inside it. The removability grounds contain no character credit; good moral character gates benefits and relief only. A single ordinary DUI is not a deportability ground (Leocal; Lopez-Meza). Deportability has no statute of limitations; only naturalization ends a resident’s exposure. ICE removed 271,484 people in fiscal 2024, 32.7 percent with convictions or pending charges; the interior cut ran 93 percent criminal-involved. Europeans are removed—1,540 in fiscal 2023—under the same statute as everyone else. The public’s model is measured, not guessed: 65 percent for a requirements-based path to stay (Pew, June 2025); of the selective majority, 97 percent for deporting the violent and 15 percent for deporting the employed (Pew, February–March 2025). Precarity is monetized inside the system as a matter of adjudicated record—recruitment debt, confiscated passports, and deportation threats priced by juries and courts in the Signal and Global Horizons cases. The smuggler’s fee is documented in the sentencing record at $6,500 to $18,000 a person, with the unpaid held in stash houses until it was paid (Renoj-Matul, sentenced to 262 months; Mejia-Zuniga, ten years). At the brand-name end of the food and leisure industries, the exploited worker is on a contractor’s payroll, not the brand’s: PSSI, Fayette, Exel, Cal-Clean, HCL, and Cognizant are where the penalties and settlements in the file land.
Wrongful arrests, detentions, and removals of potential citizens: 674 arrested, 121 detained, 70 removed, fiscal 2015–2020, by the GAO’s audit, whose own caveats make the counts floors. European removals: 1,540 of 183,360 formal removals in fiscal 2023, under 1 percent, against about 61,000 European visa-waiver overstays in fiscal 2024. The Abrego Garcia removal: one case, fully documented, error conceded by the agency in court. Deaths in ICE custody: 38 in fiscal 2026, the highest year in the agency’s series, against tens of thousands detained on any given day. Documented voluntary departures: 6,118 court grants in the first six months of 2025—a real channel, at documented scale. Adjudicated exploitation: more than $14 million awarded in David v. Signal International (2015); $8.7 million and $7,658,500 in the Global Horizons cases (2014–2016); 1,558 labor-trafficking situations identified by the national hotline in 2023—floors, built only from cases that reached an authority. The case record of section 14, each item bounded by its instrument: a 54-count indictment of twenty-four defendants and more than $200 million in alleged proceeds in United States v. Patricio, resolved by guilty pleas running from a year and a day for the first-named defendant to thirty years in the related Mendoza case; $1,544,076 in penalties against PSSI for 102 children on overnight sanitation shifts, and $649,304 against Fayette Janitorial for at least twenty-four, with a criminal indictment of Fayette personnel unsealed in 2025 and untried at filing; $164,814 settled by Mar-Jac Poultry after the death of a sixteen-year-old on its sanitation shift, and $385,000 assessed against its Alabama plant for minors as young as thirteen; 188 months for the leader of the Ohio egg-farm ring that held eight Guatemalan minors against their paychecks; New York’s nail-salon task force ordering $2 million to 652 workers in its first year; $213,042 in back wages recovered for 1,028 J-1 students at the Hershey warehouse; and the J-1 au pair sponsors’ $65.5 million settlement in Beltran, paid without adjudication of the wage-fixing alleged.
DHS’s count of 1.6–1.9 million “self-deportations” in 2025: built on survey population estimates, with no published methodology or departure count beneath it. The claim of a million-scale population of unlawfully present Ukrainians and Eastern Europeans: no DHS table at scale supports it; the measured European overstay stock is real and smaller, and most post-2022 Ukrainians hold parole or TPS. The “80 percent” non-criminal share as a constant of the system: no official series states it; the measured series runs 41 percent non-convicted (fiscal 2013) to roughly two-thirds (fiscal 2024) and higher in 2025. The department’s 622,000-deportations claim for 2025 as a figure comparable to the ICE removal series. That elections—or removals—are administered on any basis other than the statutory one, asserted without an instrument: no specimen at scale has been produced in this file, from any direction.
That a single DUI forfeits a green card under current law: Leocal and Lopez-Meza dispose of it; the bill that would make it so, H.R. 875, passed the House in June 2025 and is not law. That criminals are put in deportation facilities instead of jail: the detainer record shows criminal custody and sentence first, ICE custody after. That the border hop resets the Schengen clock: the 90/180 rule is a rolling cumulative window. That “bad hombres” describes the removed population as a whole: the convicted have been a minority of total removals in every recent year of ICE’s published split. That wrongful removal of citizens does not occur: the GAO’s audit is the disposing instrument. That long residence alone ripens into lawful status in the United States: the registry door stands frozen at January 1, 1972, and no other provision enacts the ripening. That an adjudicated record of J-1 or H-2B exploitation by Disney at its parks exists to be cited: the desk’s search of the enforcement and court record finds none—Disney’s documented case is the 2015 replacement of its own American IT staff by a contractor’s H-1B workers, investigated and closed without a violation.

As the file stands on Sunday, November 8, 2026: deportation in the United States is an administrative process built on two statute lists—inadmissibility for those at the door, deportability for those admitted—run through a court track with hearings and appeals and three faster tracks without them, ending in bars of five, ten, and twenty years for the removed, no removal bar for the voluntarily departed, and unlawful-presence bars that turn on time accrued however a person leaves; its recent caseload is majority non-criminal in the totals and majority criminal in the interior, its overstay flow has exceeded its border flow among new arrivals for nearly two decades, its court backlog stands above three million cases, its final orders outstanding above 1.4 million, its detention population near record levels with seven in ten detainees holding no conviction, and its statute asks nothing, at the removability stage, about whether the person before it is good; the resident it holds longest is exposed for the whole of his residence to a list of tripwires that never expire until the oath of naturalization discharges them; the government’s own auditors have documented its errors against citizens at small, real scale; and every large claim in the public argument—the millions self-deported, the eighty percent, the criminal flood, the spotless machine—grades, on the instruments available, below the arithmetic the record actually keeps.

 The File, Clipped

 Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective, a source with a position, printed because it is useful, and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only part of this file stamped objective. Thirty-one items.
